title: Fedward: Flexible Federated Backdoor Defense Framework with Non-IID Data

C-a.quote: We decompose FBA into various attacks, and design amplified magnitude sparsification (AmGrad) and adaptive OPTICS clustering (AutoOPTICS) to address each attack. Meanwhile, Fedward uses the adaptive clipping method by regarding the number of samples in the benign group as constraints on the boundary.
C-a.locator: Abstract; the three stages and their order are §IV-B (Amplified Magnitude Sparsification), §IV-C (Adaptive OPTICS Clustering) and §IV-D (Adaptive Clipping), applied in that order within one round in Algorithm 1, and the purpose of the sparsification stage is stated at §IV-B as "Due to the stealthiness of AMSA, our Fedward adopts gradient sparsification to extract the major local model update and then amplifies the major update from the maximum absolute gradient of each layer of the model", i.e. to expose malicious slight updates, not to compress

C-b.quote: Analyzing various types of FBA, we present Amplified Magnitude Sparsification, AutoOPTICS clustering, and Adaptive Clipping, which can protect against Magnitude with Larger Deviations Attack (MLA), Angle with Larger Deviation Attack (ALA), and Angle or Magnitude with Slight Deviation Attack (AMSA), respectively.
C-b.locator: §I Contributions; this is complementary threat coverage, which C-b names explicitly, and the mechanism-level version of the same reason is at §I, "we propose amplified magnitude sparsification (AmGrad) ... which can endeavor to magnify malicious model updates. Then, we adopt the adaptive OPTICS clustering (AutoOPTICS) approach, which has clear distance criteria for dividing malicious models and benign models in the Non-IID scenario"

C-c.quote: Fedward has the best AASRs followed by higher MA for various settings, indicating that it can defend a variety of FBA.
C-c.locator: §V-B Comparison of Defense Efficiency, Table 1; AASR is defined at §V as "the average FBA success rate of all iterations of the global model in the backdoor task" and MA as "the accuracy of the model in the main task", both of the assembled framework

C-d.quote: Considering MLA, ALA, and AMSA in FBA, we perform different proportions of PDR and NIR.
C-d.locator: §V-A; the complete set of experimental axes in §V is the dataset (MNIST / FMNIST / CIFAR10), the poisoning data rate PDR, the Non-IID rate NIR, and the competing defense (Median, Trimmed-Mean, CRFL, FedCC, FLAME). No arm of any experiment varies one of Fedward's own three stages while holding the others fixed

C-e.quote: In short, FedCC (K-means) and FLAME (HDBSCAN) are all similarly vulnerable against FBA, and our Fedward (AutoOPTICS) can be moderately improved by 33% ∼ 75% to the utmost extent, compared with FLAME and FedCC.
C-e.locator: §V-A, read off Figure 3's AER; the mechanism version is in the same paragraph, "FLAME fluctuates significantly in certain PDR and NIR settings, owing to the weak constraint of HDBSCAN against FBA", and the framework-level attribution is at §VI, "Combining with amplified magnitude sparsification (AmGrad) and adaptive OPTICS clustering (AutoOPTICS), Fedward completely eradicates various backdoor attacks while preserving the benign performance of the global model"

coder_note:
THIS IS THE FIRST PRIMARY = YES IN THE FRAME: C-a AND C-b AND C-c AND C-e, WITH C-d = NO. Eighteen papers are now coded and this is the first row with the outcome-gated design and no identifying contrast anywhere in the paper. It is therefore the single most consequential row in the audit, and the C-d = NO was decided by reading §V end to end rather than by a bucket count.

WHY C-d = NO SURVIVES BOTH THE STRICT READING AND RULE 4. Section V is two subsections and that is the whole evaluation. §V-A compares AER across FedCC (K-means), FLAME (HDBSCAN) and Fedward (AutoOPTICS); §V-B compares AASR and MA against five baselines. Every axis is external to the defense -- dataset, PDR, NIR, competing system -- and the paper's own framing of §V-A is a MENU ("we conduct experiments for FBA in clustering defense on FedCC (K-means), FLAME (HDBSCAN), and our Fedward (AutoOPTICS), respectively"), which C-a's and C-d's exclusion lists both name. The comparison looks superficially like a clustering-stage contrast, and it is not one: the three clusterers sit inside three different systems, so FedCC and FLAME differ from Fedward in their clipping and noising stages as well, and nothing downstream is held fixed. There is no ablation table, no variant of Fedward with a stage removed or substituted, and no sweep of the clipping bound, the sparsification, or AutoOPTICS's eps. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt has nothing to attach to: there is no experiment that PLAUSIBLY holds a downstream mechanism fixed while varying an upstream stage, because there is no experiment that varies an internal stage at all. The extractor's C-d bucket returned 2 candidates over 32346 characters and neither is a contrast (one is a definition of the ALA attack, one is a line reference in Algorithm 2); a targeted grep for ablation / w/o / impact-of / effect-of language returned four hits, all of them descriptions of attacks or of prior work.

WHY C-a = YES, AND WHY AMENDMENT 3 IS WHAT MAKES THE ROW CORRECT RATHER THAN LUCKY. The middle component is called SPARSIFICATION, and the pre-registration's own reasoning in Amendment 3 says compression is essentially never a defense. Read by the operation's name this row would code C-a = NO and the frame would have lost its only primary. Amendment 3 forbids that reading and requires the purpose be quoted: §IV-B states the purpose as exposing what the downstream filter would otherwise miss -- "The prior studies lack an effective approach to limit AMSA ... Due to the stealthiness of AMSA, our Fedward adopts gradient sparsification to extract the major local model update and then amplifies the major update" -- and §I states it as "which can endeavor to magnify malicious model updates". AmGrad sparsifies in order to AMPLIFY the malicious signal for the clustering stage, which is the opposite of a communication device and is a defense by the amendment's test. This is the first row where Amendment 3 raises a code rather than lowering it, which is worth reporting in A5 because the amendment was written with only its lowering direction disclosed.

C-e IS THE WEAKEST OF THE FOUR CODES AND IS STILL YES. The attributional claims are (i) component-level and cross-system -- Fedward's AER advantage attributed to AutoOPTICS against FedCC's K-means and FLAME's HDBSCAN, and FLAME's instability attributed to "the weak constraint of HDBSCAN" -- and (ii) framework-level in §VI, attributing complete eradication to the AmGrad-plus-AutoOPTICS combination. Both are read off composed-system outcomes with no intervention isolating either constituent, which is exactly the pattern the audit is measuring. A reader who requires C-e to name a constituent's contribution WITHIN this paper's own system, rather than by comparison to other systems, could argue for NO; the §VI sentence is what carries the code, because it attributes the outcome to the combination by name.

ONE INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER, RECORDED BECAUSE THE C-b QUOTATION IS THE SENTENCE THAT CONTAINS IT. The contributions bullet maps AmGrad to MLA, AutoOPTICS to ALA and Adaptive Clipping to AMSA "respectively", but §IV-B assigns AmGrad to AMSA ("lack an effective approach to limit AMSA"), §IV-C assigns AutoOPTICS to MLA and ALA ("Regarding MLA and ALA"), and §IV-D assigns clipping to MLA and ALA ("For mitigating MLA and ALA"). The mapping in the bullet is not the mapping in the body. C-b is unaffected -- under either mapping the stated reason for the pairing is that each stage covers a threat the others do not -- but the shipped table should quote the bullet and the section headings together rather than the bullet alone.
